docs.title: Business Observability — Walk-Before-Run Kit
docs.text:
Draft — rendered 2026-07-27.

Business observability makes a business process's health explicit and traceable — from a business expectation down to the failing connection — so a team can say what "working" means for the process, and show whether it is.

docs.title: Where to begin
docs.text:
Open Run your first process. It names who to bring into the room, how the first working session runs, and what you produce.

Start on the tech side: draft what you can from your own knowledge and the service's code and docs, mark what needs business validation, and bring the business in later.

docs.title: The path
docs.text: Run your first process → the capture templates (service profile / stakeholder expectations / signal definitions) → the worked example, which shows what a finished result looks like to check your own against.

docs.title: The reasoning behind it
docs.text: • The Methodology — why observability starts from business health, not telemetry.

docs.title: The Methodology — Business Observability
docs.text: This page explains what business observability is as a methodology.

docs.title: The core claim
docs.text:
Observability begins with defining success in business health terms — not with telemetry. Traditional monitoring starts with the data you can collect (metrics, logs, traces) and layers business meaning on top when time permits. Business observability reverses that order. Business context is defined first. Signals are designed to measure that context. Everything downstream — dashboards, alerts, playbooks — derives from the business definition, not from whatever the platform happened to collect.

This ordering is a deliberate departure from the industry's common default, chosen for a testable reason: a telemetry-first practice produces comprehensive dashboards that an executive cannot use to answer "is the business healthy right now?" A business-context-first practice can.

docs.title: The Four-Layer Model
docs.text:
Layer Question it answers Primary owner Business Health Is the stakeholder expectation being met? Product Owner Business Impact How bad is it when we fail? PO + Ops / Compliance Application Is the workflow executing correctly? Developer / QA System Is the platform operational? SRE / Platform

Application and System validate the mechanism (up, fast, correct). Business Health validates the intended outcome. Business Impact quantifies the consequence when outcomes miss. A service can be green on Application and System (workflows running, infrastructure healthy) while failing on Business Health (business outcomes not met). That gap is why the business layers exist.

docs.title: The Semantic Chain
docs.text:
Every signal traces back to a business reason through an explicit chain:

[Stakeholder] has an [Expectation]
  which is measured by a [Business Health Signal]
    supported by [Application Signals] and [System Signals]
      if the expectation is breached → [Business Impact Signal]
        → [Alert] → [Owner + Next Action]

No signal exists without a stakeholder expectation it serves. No stakeholder expectation exists without a signal measuring it.

docs.title: How this relates to SRE / SLO practice
docs.text: SLO/SLI practice (Google SRE, Hidalgo) is compatible and upstream-consumed: an SLO is a quantified stakeholder expectation (Business Health). Error budgets are the reliability-velocity tradeoff made explicit within a business context. Business observability does not replace SRE — it extends it with the business-context layer that SLOs alone don't require. Teams with mature SLO practice have most of Business Health — and System/Application telemetry in abundance. What's typically missing is the structure around the SLOs: named stakeholder expectations each SLO serves, Business Impact quantification when one breaches, and the explicit linkage that ties existing telemetry into the chain.

docs.title: How this relates to telemetry pillars
docs.text: The industry-standard pillars (metrics, logs, traces, profiles) are a classification by data shape. The Four-Layer Model is a classification by business meaning. Both are valid; they answer different questions. A well-instrumented service has signals across all pillars — this methodology organizes them by layer first, pillar second.

docs.title: Service Profile Template
docs.text: The service profile is where you start: one record that names a service's identity, what it does, how critical it is, and who owns it. Everything you capture next refers back to it.

docs.title: What to capture
docs.text:
One record per service — the information a person provides:

What to capture Meaning Service name Its technical name, plus a readable display name for dashboards What it does The service's business purpose, in plain language Criticality Its tier, from 1 (most critical) to 6 (least) Business unit The owning organization Owners The product owner, and the technical owner

Your platform also links in system keys — the application id from your CMDB and the org-hierarchy placement — from your registries. Those aren't yours to invent; they're looked up.

Worked example — the ledger-writer service (Bank of Anthos):

What to capture Value Service name ledger-writer (display: Ledger Writer) What it does Validate and record every customer payment Criticality Tier 1 Business unit Payments Owners Payments product owner and technical lead

docs.title: Signal Definition Template
docs.text: Once a service and its stakeholder expectations exist, signals are what measure whether those expectations are being met. Each signal sits at one of four layers — a Business Health signal measures an expectation; Application and System signals support and explain it; a Business Impact signal quantifies the consequence when an expectation breaches.

docs.title: What to capture
docs.text:
One record per signal — the information a person provides:

What to capture Meaning Signal name A readable name for dashboards (e.g., Transaction Success Rate) Which layer System, Application, Business Health, or Business Impact — it follows from what the signal measures: a signal on a stakeholder expectation is Business Health; a diagnostic that explains one is Application or System What it means In business terms, and how it is measured Target The SLO target and the time window it applies to — for success-rate and threshold signals; a business-impact signal quantifies consequence and carries no target

The signal's kind — a success-rate, a threshold, or a business-impact measure — follows from what you are measuring, and each kind carries its own measurement details (a ratio needs a numerator and denominator; a threshold needs an operator, value, and unit). In practice the product owner names the signal and its target, the developer fills in how it is measured, and the platform configures alerting.

Each signal stays tied to the expectation it measures, so you can always check which expectations still have no signal.

docs.title: Stakeholder Expectation Template
docs.text: Stakeholder expectations capture who cares about a service and what they need — 3-5 per service, each a complete story: "As [stakeholder], I expect [X]. If broken: [impact]." The 3-5 limit forces you to decide what matters most.

docs.title: What to capture
docs.text:
What to capture Meaning Stakeholder Who cares — a named role (e.g., Bank Customers) Expectation What they expect, in their words Impact category One of: customer experience, financial, legal / risk, operational Impact The consequence if the expectation breaks Priority Critical, High, Medium, or Low

Worked example — one expectation on the ledger-writer service (Bank of Anthos):

What to capture Value Stakeholder Bank Customers Expectation Payments complete successfully, quickly, and without double-charging Impact category Customer experience Impact The only path to send money is down — no fallback Priority Critical

docs.title: Run your team's first process
docs.text:
One facilitated working session — about 90 minutes — turns a business process you pick into your first service profile: what the process owes, to whom, and the signals that show whether it's holding. This page is the run sheet. Run it once with facilitation; after that your team runs its own.

New to the idea? Read the why first.

Why business observability explains why observability starts from business health, not telemetry. This page is the how — it assumes you're sold on the idea and ready to do it.

docs.title: Before the session
docs.text:
Get four things ready. None needs tooling; two go faster with it.

1 — Pick one business process. One the business notices when it fails, and one the team knows well. A good first pick beats a perfect one.

2 — Get three people in the room (however your org names the roles):

  • Business — knows what the process owes and to whom (product owner, BA, or the ops lead who fields the complaints).
  • Engineering — knows the applications inside the process.
  • Monitoring — owns today's alerts for those applications.

3 — Build the process inventory. One table: the process → every application that participates, in order → where each runs. Pull it from architecture docs and runbooks; if none exist, write it from the engineers' heads. Most teams find this table exists nowhere — producing it is your first real output, not prep overhead.

4 — Get the code-level picture in front of the engineers. Run DeepWiki (a tool that reads a repo and builds a readable wiki of how the code works) against the applications' repos for flow diagrams and service descriptions, then have the engineers correct it — the documented flow must match the real one before anything is measured against it. No tooling yet? A hand-drawn flow the engineers agree on works for process one.

Then read the worked example — it shows what "done" looks like, so the room can check its own output against it.

No room yet? Start solo.

Draft the stakeholder chains yourself from documents and your own knowledge, in the session order below — and mark every expectation and signal NEEDS VALIDATION. A solo pass is a draft, not a finished profile. The session then runs as confirm-and-correct — faster than starting blank, and nothing self-answered slips through as settled.

docs.title: The session — 90 minutes
docs.text:
One person facilitates and asks; the room answers. Run the segments in this order — it follows how business people actually reason, so traceability builds as you go instead of being reconnected afterward.

# Segment Time You walk out with 1 Context 10 min the inventory table, confirmed in the room 2 Stakeholder chains — the core 50 min one closed chain per stakeholder 3 Impact 10 min a cost attached to each expectation 4 Technical signals 15 min existing monitors connected upward 5 Close 5 min open questions, each with an owner and a date

docs.title: 1 · Context — 10 min
docs.text: What is this process, what does it participate in, who depends on it. Confirm the inventory table in the room.

docs.title: 2 · Stakeholder chains — 50 min · the core
docs.text:
One stakeholder at a time, complete before moving on:

  • Who are they? A named role — the operations team, the downstream reconciliation group, the customer.
  • What do they expect of this process, as a measurable sentence? ("Files arrive by 6am." "A transaction completes end to end in 10 seconds.")
  • What signal would tell us each expectation is met or missed? Name it, even if nothing measures it today.
  • Close the chain before the next stakeholder: does every expectation have a signal? Gaps stay on the page as gaps.

docs.title: 3 · Impact — 10 min
docs.text: When each expectation is missed, what does it cost — money, customers, regulatory exposure, downstream teams blocked? Attach the cost to the expectation it belongs to.

docs.title: 4 · Technical signals — 15 min
docs.text: Now bring in the engineers: for each business signal, which application-level signals would explain a breach (workflow errors, queue depth, latency A→B)? Which system-level signals sit under those? This is where years of bottom-up monitoring get connected upward instead of thrown away.

docs.title: 5 · Close — 5 min
docs.text:
Read back every question the room couldn't answer — each with an owner and a date.

The session's output

A filled service profile: stakeholders → expectations → business signals → supporting application and system signals, plus impact notes and the gap list.

docs.title: After the session
docs.text:
Set measurements and targets. For each signal: which source answers it — logs, APM, synthetics — and what the target is. Where no target was ever agreed, derive a starting range from what "normal" has looked like over recent months, alert on deviation, and replace it with a real agreement when one exists.

Wire the response. Every signal that can breach gets an owner and a next action. From here it's the reliability practice you already run — now anchored to the process map instead of tribal memory.

Let the profile drive the artifacts. The filled profile is the source dashboards, alerts, and playbooks generate from. Until that machinery is local: keep the profile on a wiki page, build the dashboard once by hand from it, and map question → signal → tool.

docs.title: Process two and three
docs.text: Run the next process with less facilitation — the people from session one can now lead their own. Log friction as it happens (what confused the room, what blocked progress — 30 seconds an entry) and fix the next run from the log. A signal that traces to no expectation is a cleanup candidate, not a keeper.

docs.title: What this is
docs.text:
The completed output of a first-process run — the filled service profile that a first-process run produces — for a real service: the ledger-writer service of Bank of Anthos, a public reference banking application. Use it two ways: read it before your own session to see what done looks like, and compare your session's output against it afterward.

This page keeps the shape your session produces: stakeholders → expectations → business signals → supporting application and system signals, plus impact notes and the gap list.

docs.title: The service in one paragraph
docs.text: Ledger-writer validates and records every customer payment — the single gate through which all payments flow. It is critical-path: there is no alternative channel, no degraded mode, no retry queue. When it fails, customers experience immediate, total inability to send money. Tier 1; regulatory exposure: every transaction must produce an auditable record.

docs.title: The process it serves
docs.text: Send Payment: payment initiation (frontend) → transaction acceptance (ledger-writer — the step this profile covers, blocking) → balance update (balance-reader) → payment confirmation (frontend). Critical dependencies at the acceptance step: the balance-reader service (synchronous call, no fallback) and the ledger database (synchronous write, no queue).

docs.title: Stakeholder chains — the session's core output
docs.text: Four chains. Each one: who → what they expect (as a measurable sentence) → the business health signal that tells us it's met or missed → what it costs when it isn't.

docs.title: Chain 1 — Bank Customers (CRITICAL)
docs.text:
Expectation: "Payments complete successfully, quickly, and without double-charging."

Business health signal Question it answers Target Transaction Success Rate Are customer payments completing successfully? ≥ 99.5% (30-day) Transaction Processing Duration p95 Is payment processing fast enough? < 2,000 ms Payment Volume Capacity Headroom Can we absorb volume spikes (payroll day, month-end)? ≥ 20% buffer

Impact when missed: the only path for sending money is down — no fallback; roughly $2,400/hour of uncaptured revenue at baseline volume; beyond 2 seconds customers resubmit, which stresses duplicate prevention; trust erosion and account-closure risk.

docs.title: Chain 2 — Compliance & Risk Management (CRITICAL)
docs.text:
Expectation: "Every processed transaction produces a complete, auditable record; no unauthorized transactions are accepted."

Business health signal Question it answers Target Transaction Audit Completeness Does every transaction — including rejected ones — produce a complete audit record? ≥ 99.99%

Impact when missed: audit gaps are examination findings — BSA/AML reporting gaps, consent-order risk, mandatory disclosure. The record must show why a transaction was rejected, not just that it was.

docs.title: Chain 3 — Finance & Treasury (HIGH)
docs.text:
Expectation: "Ledger balances are accurate — no duplicate entries, no missing transactions, reconciliation closes daily."

Business health signal Question it answers Target Duplicate Prevention Rate Are duplicate payment attempts caught before ledger write? ≥ 99.9%

Impact when missed: at just 0.1% leakage, ~5 duplicate transactions a day each need manual reversal; balance errors, daily reconciliation breaks, restatement risk.

docs.title: Chain 4 — Payments Operations (HIGH)
docs.text:
Expectation: "Transaction failures are visible and diagnosable within 15 minutes; the system handles volume changes without manual intervention."

This chain is served by the whole signal set plus the diagnostic descent below — and it carries this profile's most instructive finding: no single composite health signal exists; operators must correlate individual signals. That finding is recorded in the gap list rather than hidden.

Impact when missed: blind spots in payment health, manual-correlation delay, incident-response SLA breaches, dependency failures cascading undetected.

docs.title: The supporting layers — connecting existing monitoring upward
docs.text:
Every business health signal above is explained by signals at the layers below. This is where a team's existing monitors slot in instead of being thrown away.

Application-layer signals (which step is failing?):

Signal Question it answers Explains Payment Validation Rate Are payments passing the validation chain (auth, format, business rules)? Success Rate Balance Check Latency p95 Is the balance-verification dependency fast enough? (target < 500 ms) Duration, Success Rate Ledger Write Latency p95 Is the database write keeping up? (target < 200 ms) Duration, Success Rate Transaction Request Rate What volume is arriving right now? Capacity Headroom

System-layer signals (why is it failing?):

Signal Question it answers Ledger-Writer Availability Is the service accepting requests at all? (readiness probe) CPU Utilization Is it working past its resource budget? (target < 70%) DB Connection Pool Saturation Is the write path about to bottleneck? (target < 80%)

docs.title: How diagnosis walks the layers
docs.text: Business health says customers can't pay or payments are slow. Application signals say which step — validation, balance check, or write. System signals say why — service down, CPU contention, pool exhausted. For this service the single largest risk is the balance-reader dependency: its failure blocks every local payment and surfaces as ledger-writer errors, not as a clear dependency signal.

docs.title: The gap list — kept on the page as gaps
docs.text:
What the analysis could not settle, recorded instead of smoothed over:

  • Duplicate prevention has a structural hole: the deduplication cache is per-pod, not shared — a pod restart or a multi-replica deployment opens a window for duplicate writes. (Recorded as a violated precondition.)
  • Rated capacity has never been established by load test — the capacity-headroom signal depends on it. (Unknown.)
  • Whether balance-reader scales with ledger-writer throughput is unverified — if it's the bottleneck, headroom overstates safety. (Unknown.)
  • No composite health signal — Operations correlates individual signals by hand today.

docs.title: What to imitate
docs.text:
• Every expectation is a measurable sentence, not a sentiment.
  • Every expectation has a named signal — even where nothing measures it yet; the gap stays visible.
  • Every signal carries the question it answers, in business language.
  • Existing monitors are connected upward under business signals, not discarded.
  • Gaps stay on the page as gaps — the profile records what the room couldn't answer.
